opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think inference scaling is one of the most exciting shifts we've seen recently. For a long time the story was about pre-training: more data, more parameters, more compute, and you get more capable models. That's still true, but we're running into the limits of high-quality human data. Inference-time compute opens a second axis. Instead of only making the model bigger, you let it think longer, search over possibilities, try things, and check its own work before committing to an answer.

What interests me most is how this connects to open-endedness, which has been central to my research. If you look at how humans make progress in science or mathematics, it's rarely one forward pass. It's a long process of generating hypotheses, testing them, getting feedback, and building on stepping stones that weren't obviously useful at first. Inference scaling starts to give models a way to do something similar. You can sample many candidate solutions, use a verifier or the environment to tell you which ones are promising, and refine from there.

The key ingredient is feedback. Spending more compute at inference is only useful if you have some signal for telling good outcomes from bad ones. In domains like code or math, where you can run tests or check proofs, the gains can be dramatic. In more open-ended domains it's harder, and I think that's where a lot of the interesting research questions are. How do you get a reliable signal of what's interesting, novel, or useful when there isn't a ground-truth checker? Here, models judging other models, or a notion of interestingness learned from human data, could play a big role.

I also think there's a nice loop between inference-time and training-time compute. Once you've spent a lot of compute at inference to discover a good solution, you can distill that back into the model so the next generation starts from a higher baseline. That's very reminiscent of AlphaGo-style self-improvement, where search produces better data and better data produces a better policy. If we can get that loop working robustly beyond narrow domains, I think it's a credible path toward systems that keep discovering new things rather than just interpolating what's on the internet.

So for me, inference scaling isn't just a trick for squeezing a few more benchmark points out of a model. It's a step toward models that actively explore and generate new knowledge. That's ultimately what we'd want from something we'd call superhuman intelligence.

r001.rationale: It contrasts making the model bigger with spending more inference-time compute to think longer, search, and check work.

r002.rationale: It does not distinguish using information in a large context window from merely accepting many input tokens.

r003.rationale: It mentions refining candidate solutions, but does not say this happens through iteration within the model’s context window.

r004.rationale: It compares inference scaling to scientific progress, but does not describe an outer loop around the language model in AI Scientist systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think inference scaling is one of the most exciting shifts we've seen, because for a long time the whole story was about training. Scale up the data, scale up the parameters, scale up the compute, and you get a better model. That still holds, but it's expensive and it's slow, and at some point you run into the limits of what you can get out of a fixed, static set of weights.

What inference scaling says is that you don't have to bake all of the capability into the forward pass. You can let the model spend more compute at test time, and you can trade that compute for better answers. That can take many forms. The simplest version is just sampling more, generating many candidates and selecting among them. Then you get chain of thought, where the model externalizes its reasoning and effectively gives itself more steps to work with. And then you move into search, where the model is exploring a tree of possibilities, backtracking, verifying, and refining, much more like how we think about planning in reinforcement learning than how we traditionally thought about language modeling.

The reason I find this compelling is that it lines up with how intelligence works more broadly. A chess player doesn't play at the same level in a blitz game as in a classical game, and the difference is purely how much time they get to think. Giving models that same flexibility, where easy problems get a quick answer and hard problems get a long deliberation, feels like the right abstraction.

There's also a nice connection to open-endedness, which is where a lot of my own work sits. If a model can generate candidates, evaluate them, and iterate, then you have the ingredients for a system that improves itself at test time rather than only at training time. You can have the model propose solutions, critique them, try variations, and keep the ones that work. That's essentially an evolutionary or search process running on top of the language model, and it extends what the model can do well beyond what you'd get from a single pass.

The important caveat is that inference scaling only buys you something if you have a reliable signal to scale against. If you're sampling a hundred answers and you can't tell which one is right, you've just spent a hundred times the compute for nothing. So verification, whether that's a learned verifier, a formal check, code execution, or a simulated environment that gives you ground truth, becomes the bottleneck. In domains like mathematics and programming it's relatively easy to get that signal, which is why we've seen such rapid progress there. In more open-ended domains it's much harder, and I think that's where a lot of the interesting research is right now.

And the last thing I'd say is that these aren't independent axes. Whatever the model learns to do at inference time, with search and self-correction, can be distilled back into the next generation of training. So you get a loop where inference scaling produces better data, better data produces a stronger base model, and the stronger base model makes inference scaling even more effective. That flywheel is, to me, the really interesting part.

r001.rationale: It contrasts putting capability into fixed weights with spending more compute at test time.

r002.rationale: It does not distinguish using information in a large context window from merely accepting many input tokens.

r003.rationale: It describes critiquing and varying candidate outputs iteratively, but does not say this refinement happens within the model’s context window.

r004.rationale: It mentions search and iteration on top of a language model, but does not describe an AI Scientist system’s scientific workflow as an outer loop.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting thing about inference scaling is that it gives us another axis along which to improve these systems. We’ve put a lot of emphasis on scaling training—more data, larger models, more compute. But once you have a trained model, there’s still the question of how much computation you allow it to use to solve a particular problem.

For a simple question, you might want an immediate answer. For a difficult reasoning problem, it can be useful to generate several candidate solutions, check them, and revise an approach that isn’t working. So the model becomes part of a larger process that can spend additional effort where it’s useful.

The crucial point is that more computation doesn’t automatically mean a better answer. You need some way of determining whether you’re making progress. With code, for example, you can run tests. In other settings, evaluating a proposed solution can be almost as difficult as producing it. And if your checking mechanism is unreliable, you can spend a lot of computation reinforcing a mistake.

So I see inference scaling as very promising, particularly when there’s useful feedback. But the interesting research question is how we train systems to use that extra computation effectively—to explore alternatives, recognize errors, and know when further thinking is actually worthwhile.

r001.rationale: It contrasts scaling training with allowing a trained model more computation to solve a particular problem.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss context-window capacity or distinguish using information in a large window from accepting many input tokens.

r003.rationale: It describes generating, checking, and revising candidate solutions, but does not say this refinement occurs within the model’s context window.

r004.rationale: It does not mention AI Scientist systems or describe a scientific workflow as an outer loop around a language model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting thing about inference scaling is that it gives us another axis for improving these systems. Instead of asking a model to produce an answer immediately, you can give it more computation to explore different approaches, check intermediate steps, and revise its answer.

But the important question is what makes that additional computation useful. Just generating more tokens doesn’t necessarily get you a better answer. You need some way of distinguishing progress from going down the wrong path. In coding, for example, you can run tests. In mathematics, you might be able to verify a solution. That feedback makes search much more powerful.

So I see training and inference scaling as complementary. Training can teach a model how to use additional computation effectively, and then at inference time you can spend more computation on a particularly difficult problem. The interesting challenge is extending that beyond domains where checking the answer is straightforward.
